story:
Milan sat with Dad at the big sports arena. The seats were so high up. Milan looked down at the players. They ran like fast little bees.

Milan wanted to be tall like the players. Before the game, Dad measured him on the wall. Milan stood up very straight. The mark was right by his ear.

The game was long and fun. Milan clapped for the team in snowy white shirts. He watched them jump and score. Then it was time to go home.

At home, Dad measured Milan again. Milan stood up straight, just like before. But the new mark was lower! "Why am I smaller?" Milan asked. He had stood tall all day at the game. Maybe standing and sitting all day had squished him down, just a little.

The next morning, Milan ran to the wall. He measured himself right away. The mark was high again, higher than at night! "I grew back!" Milan said. He was tall in the morning, and small at night. What a strange thing to notice.

Peyton sat in music class with a small drum. Today was singing day. The song was about a horse. A silly, bouncy horse who liked to trot and trot.

"Sing it high!" said her teacher. Peyton sang high. Then she sang higher. Then she sang so high her friend Mia laughed. Peyton laughed too. They sang the horse song again and again. High, higher, highest!

At snack time, the class watched bread dough in a bowl. It sat on the table, small and flat. Peyton peeked at it after music class. The dough was big now. Big and puffy, like a pillow! "It grew!" said Peyton. "Maybe it is alive!"

Her teacher smiled and did not explain. Later, they got to bake the bread. It smelled warm and sweet. Peyton watched it rise in the oven too. "It keeps growing," she said. "Something inside it must be working." She grinned, proud of her big idea.

Theodore went to the World Fair at his community center. Flags from many countries hung on the wall. A helper named Miss Lin gave him a paper passport. "There are about 195 countries in the world," she said. "You cannot visit them all today. But you can try a few!"

Theodore had a plan. First, he would find a flag. Next, he would match it to a country on the map. Then, he would try a snack from that country. Last, he would get a sticker in his passport. He matched a red flag with white stripes to Russia. "Russia is so big," Miss Lin said, "it stretches across 11 time zones!" Theodore's eyes went wide. He was surprised a country could be that huge.

Then he found a tiny flag with yellow and white stripes. It was Vatican City. "That one is the smallest," said Miss Lin. "You could walk across it in about 20 minutes." Theodore giggled. "Bigger than my whole town, and smaller than my street!"

By the end, frost was forming on the windows outside. Theodore had five stickers in his passport. He held it up proudly. "I did not visit every country," he said, "but I visited enough for today."

Elliot walked into his new classroom and held his mom's hand tight.

The teacher, Ms. Reyes, smiled at him. "You can sit by the window, Elliot." He sat down and looked outside. There was frost on the grass, all white and sparkly. He watched it until class started.

At circle time, Ms. Reyes gave everyone a job. "First, find a partner. Next, walk across the room counting your steps. Then, write down your number. Last, we will compare." Elliot found his friend Sam. Elliot walked and counted twelve steps. Sam walked the same room and counted fourteen steps.

"That's wrong," said Sam. "It's the same room!" Elliot looked confused too. Ms. Reyes laughed gently. "Your feet are not the same size," she said. "That is why we use rulers instead. Every centimeter on a ruler is the same, everywhere." She handed them a ruler to try. Elliot measured the rug edge, and Sam measured it too. This time, they both got the same number.

"It matched!" Elliot said, and grinned. Counting steps felt useless now, but the ruler felt like magic. He decided he loved school already.

Owen sat at the kitchen table with a shoebox full of buttons, beads, and scraps of fabric. He wanted to make a card for his dog Biscuit, who had been his loyal friend since Owen was a baby. He dumped everything out and started to sort the pile into groups: round things in one corner, sparkly things in another, and soft fuzzy bits in the middle. But some pieces fit two groups at once, like a round sparkly button, and Owen had to decide where it belonged.

While he worked, he remembered the walk he took with Biscuit that morning through the tall grass behind his house. When they got home, Owen had found tiny green burrs stuck all over Biscuit's fur, clinging to the loops like they never wanted to let go. He had picked at them for ten whole minutes, and his fingers still smelled like grass.

Owen looked down at his craft pile and noticed something strange. One scrap of fabric had tiny loops woven into it, and a plastic hook from an old costume was sitting right next to it. He pressed the hook against the loops just to see what would happen, and it caught, just like the burrs had caught on Biscuit's fur.

Owen grinned and pressed it again, testing it three more times to make sure it wasn't an accident. He glued the hook and the loop scrap onto the card so the flap would open and close without tape. When he showed his mom, she laughed and said, "That's basically Velcro, you know." Owen just smiled, already wondering what else in the world worked like a burr.

Henry gripped the sides of the wooden boat and grinned so hard his cheeks hurt. He had flown all the way to Venice, Italy, with his grandmother to see his cousin's christening, and now he was riding to church in a boat instead of a car. The water smelled like salt and old stone, and it slapped gently against the sides of the boat, going *slap, slap, slap*, like a friendly drum.

"Where are all the cars?" Henry asked, twisting around to look at the narrow streets zooming past.

His grandmother laughed. "There are none here, silly. This whole old city sits on more than a hundred little islands, all stuck together with bridges. Everything moves by boat. Mail, groceries, even ambulances."

Henry's eyes went wide. He watched a boy about his own age zoom by, standing up and rowing a flat little boat piled high with bread and boxes of pasta. That was the grocery delivery! Henry had expected a bike with a squeaky basket, not a boy rowing like it was the most normal thing in the world. He decided that boy was pretty daring, balancing like that without falling in.

At the church, the ceremony was long and full of candles and singing that echoed off the walls like it was bouncing off water too. Henry tried to sit still, but his mind kept sorting the strange, wonderful facts of Venice. Boats for mail. Boats for milk. Boats for babies getting christened, probably. He decided Venice combined two things he loved separately, boats and cities, into one amazing place.

After the ceremony, everyone gathered outside for cake and lemonade. Henry spotted a stray cat winding between people's ankles, and he pointed it out to his cousin. "Is that the only mammal that lives on water streets?" he asked, half joking.

His cousin snorted. "There are dogs too. They just don't like getting their paws wet."

Henry laughed so hard he nearly dropped his cake. Somewhere behind them, an ambulance boat zipped by with its light spinning, cutting smoothly through the water like it belonged there, because it did.

Dylan's marimba mallets kept sliding out of his sweaty hands, which was not a great start to his third lesson at the Riverbend Community Center.

"You're gripping like you're trying to strangle them," said Priya, who sat at the marimba next to his, effortlessly rolling out a scale. She was twelve and had been playing for two years, which in Dylan's mind made her basically a professional. "Loosen up. It's a new concept for you, that's all. Give it time."

Dylan tried to loosen up, but his mallets still bounced everywhere, and the sheet music in front of him looked like a fence full of angry bees. Learning to read the notes had seemed simple enough when Ms. Alvarez explained it, but seeing the shapes on the page and turning them into sounds with his hands felt like two different languages that refused to talk to each other. He had signed up for the after school music program voluntarily, nobody made him do it, but some days he wondered why he had bothered.

During the break, Dylan and Priya wandered outside to the little footbridge behind the center, where the creek ran under old wooden planks and, further down the tracks, a freight train sometimes rumbled through around four o'clock. Dylan flopped onto the bridge railing, tired and a little discouraged, and pressed his forehead against the cool metal without really thinking about it.

That was when he heard it: a low, steady humming through the rail, faint but unmistakable, like the bridge itself was groaning softly. He sat up fast.

"Priya, listen to this," he said, tugging her sleeve toward the metal railing. She pressed her ear against it too, and her eyebrows shot up.

"I can hear the train," she whispered, "but I can't see it anywhere."

Dylan strained his eyes down the tracks. Nothing. No headlight, no rumble in the air, nothing but sparrows arguing in a nearby tree. He waited, counting under his breath the way he counted rests in his music, one Mississippi, two Mississippi, and somewhere around twenty Mississippi, he finally heard the whistle blow through the actual air, and a few seconds after that, the train itself appeared around the bend.

"That's so weird," Priya said. "It's like the metal told us before the air did."

"Maybe sound just moves faster through the rail," Dylan said, testing the idea out loud, half expecting Priya to laugh at him.

She didn't laugh. She just looked impressed, which felt even better.

Back inside, Dylan picked up his mallets again, and this time when he looked at the notes, he thought about the vibrating rail, how something invisible could travel through solid material and arrive early if you just knew where to listen. Reading music wasn't so different, he decided. The notes were quiet until you found the right way to feel them.

"Ready to try the scale again?" Ms. Alvarez asked.

Dylan nodded, gripped the mallets a little looser this time, and struck the first note clean and true.

Anthony lined up six glass bottles on Grandma's kitchen table, each one holding a different amount of water, and reached for a wooden spoon. He had seen a video where someone tapped bottles like this and played a real melody, and he wanted to make his own before Grandma's birthday dinner that evening. He tapped the first bottle, the one nearly full, and got a low, mellow bong. The nearly empty one rang out high and bright when he tapped it. "So more water means a lower note," he said to himself, feeling proud of the pattern. He tried to hypothesize a full scale, adding water bottle by bottle until the tones climbed neatly from low to high.

Grandma shuffled in wearing her apron, sniffing the air like she expected cookies instead of chimes. "That's a fine little orchestra," she said, "but have you tried blowing across the tops instead of banging on them?"

Anthony pressed his lips to the bottle with the least water and blew. A low, hollow hoot came out, nothing like the bright ping he'd gotten from tapping it. He tried the fullest bottle next, expecting an even lower groan, and instead got a note so high it made Grandma's cat leap off the windowsill. He blinked, tried it again, and got the same backward result. "Wait," he muttered, "that makes no sense. Tapping this one is high, but blowing it is low. It's exactly flipped."

He spent the next twenty minutes running back and forth between tapping and blowing, scribbling notes on a napkin like a scientist chasing a stubborn signal. Grandma pulled a tray of biscuits from the oven and set it to cool, watching him with the patient look of someone who had once been thirteen and just as puzzled by ordinary things. "Sounds like you're having a little revolution in there," she teased, tapping her own temple, "everything turning upside down at once." Anthony laughed, because that was exactly what it felt like, his whole tidy theory spinning in the opposite direction. By the time the biscuits were ready to eat, he had a coherent chart taped to the fridge, one column for tapping, one for blowing, arrows pointing opposite ways. He grinned at his grandmother, grabbed a warm biscuit, and blew one last long, high note across the fullest bottle just to hear it again.

Zoey set her backpack down on Priya's kitchen counter and pulled out the chemistry worksheet that had been bothering her since Tuesday. It was a question about boiling points, and the answer key said something that seemed impossible: that water did not always boil at exactly one hundred degrees Celsius. She had underlined the sentence three times, as if repetition might make it click.

"My uncle went to Peru last year," Priya said, rummaging through a cabinet for the good mugs, the ones without chips. "He kept complaining that his rice wouldn't cook right. Said he boiled it for way longer than normal and it still crunched between his teeth."

Zoey looked up. "Where in Peru?"

"Somewhere in the mountains. Cusco, I think." Priya shrugged like this was a minor detail, a story her uncle liked to repeat at every holiday dinner until it had become almost background noise, the kind of family tale that gets perpetuated more out of habit than interest.

Zoey pulled her laptop over and typed a search, half expecting the internet to contradict her worksheet. Instead, it confirmed something stranger: at high elevation, water boils below one hundred degrees, which explained why food left in it stays stubborn and undercooked no matter how patiently you wait. She thought about that for a moment, turning it over like a stone she'd found on a trail. If lower pressure meant a lower boiling point, then higher pressure should mean the opposite.

"Do you have a pressure cooker?" she asked.

Priya's mom kept one in the pantry, a heavy metal pot with a rubber gasket and a little weighted valve on top that looked almost decorative. Zoey set it on the stove, filled it with water, and clamped the lid down the way the instructions on the side suggested. She wanted to test her own reasoning, not just read about it: if the cooker doubled the pressure inside, water trapped in there should boil around one hundred twenty degrees instead of the usual hundred. She dropped in a handful of raw carrots for a control, since carrots took forever normally, and started the timer on her phone.

While they waited, Priya swung idly on a stool, its legs tilting back and forth like a slow pendulum, and asked whether the carrots would just dissolve into mush if the water got that much hotter. Zoey admitted she wasn't sure, but the timer would tell them soon enough, and there was something satisfying about not already knowing the ending.

Eight minutes later, the valve on top began to hiss, and Zoey killed the heat, letting the pressure ease down slowly rather than risk a startled cloud of steam. When she finally lifted the lid, the carrots slid apart under her fork with almost no resistance at all, cooked through in a fraction of the usual time. She thought back to Priya's uncle, standing at some campsite thousands of feet above sea level, stirring a pot of rice that refused to soften no matter how long he waited, probably assuming his stove was broken or his rice was bad. It hadn't been either. The difference, she realized, wasn't in the food or the flame, but in the air pressing down, or failing to press down, on the water itself. Any error in his cooking time had been negligible next to that one overlooked variable, and she wrote a note in the margin of her worksheet before closing it: pressure changes everything, even when the fire looks the same.

Hunter's laptop balanced on a stack of textbooks at the edge of Marcus's desk, the screen glowing with a half-finished program that refused to run.

"It keeps saying syntax error on line six," Hunter said, scrolling back through the code he'd copied from a tutorial video. "But I typed it exactly right."

Marcus leaned over, scanning the lines with the calm patience of someone who had made this exact mistake a dozen times already. "You're missing a colon after your if statement. Python's picky like that. One little mark and it falls apart."

Hunter added the colon, hit run, and watched the little black terminal window print out the message he'd been chasing for twenty minutes: *Welcome to the guessing game.* He grinned, feeling the small, specific triumph of something finally working. "Okay, what if I change the number it's guessing? Like, what if I make it guess higher than a hundred?"

"Try it," Marcus said, already reaching for his phone, which had just buzzed with an email notification.

Hunter changed the range in the code, from a hundred to a thousand, just to see what would happen, reasoning that if the program could handle small numbers it ought to handle bigger ones the same way. It did, without complaint, and he nodded to himself, satisfied that he understood at least one small rule of how the thing worked: change one variable, watch the result, and you learn something true about the whole system.

"Dude, look at this," Marcus said, turning his phone around. It was an email from some old gaming forum he'd signed up for years ago, the kind of site that had probably been built by one person in their bedroom. The subject line read *Your password has been sent* and the body of the email spelled out, in plain text, the exact password Marcus said he still used for half his accounts.

Hunter stared at it. "Wait, they just emailed it to you? Like, the actual password?"

"Yeah, I forgot it and clicked the link and it just came right back to me."

"That's not supposed to happen though." Hunter thought about the login system Marcus's older brother had once shown them, the one where forgetting your password meant getting a link to make a new one instead of getting the old one back. "If a site can send you your actual password, that means they're storing it somewhere just sitting there, like unlocked. Real sites scramble it into something you can't turn back into the original, so even they can't read it. That's why you always have to *reset* it instead of them just telling you what it was."

Marcus shrugged, halfway between alarmed and unbothered. "I mean, it's just my gaming forum password."

"Is it the same one you use for your email?"

Marcus's cordial expression faltered for a second, the kind of pause that answered the question better than words could.

"Change it," Hunter said. "Tonight. Not tomorrow."

Marcus groaned but opened a new tab, and Hunter went back to his own screen, typing in a fresh line of code just to test something, an idea forming the way ideas do when one true thing makes you suspicious of everything nearby. He wasn't sure yet how hashing actually worked under the hood, but he understood the shape of it now, the way your body builds an antibody after meeting a threat once and remembers how to fight it the next time. He'd met this one. He wasn't going to forget it.

The debate stage in Mr. Aldrin's third period class was really just two desks dragged to the front of the room, but Olivier had rehearsed his opening line in the bathroom mirror that morning like it mattered.

"The greenhouse effect is fake," said Trevor Nguyen, arms folded like a man who had already won. "It's propaganda. If it were real, we'd all be dead by now, roasting."

Olivier felt the familiar itch of an argument built on a shaky foundation, the kind that could be nullified with one well-placed fact if you knew where to press. He didn't know exactly where yet. That was the annoying part. He'd read three articles the night before, skimmed a textbook chapter, and watched half a video before his sister took the laptop, and none of it had assembled itself into a clean rebuttal.

"Explain the volcano thing then," Trevor said, which wasn't actually an argument, just a foible of his debating style, throwing out unrelated facts to see what stuck. "Volcanoes put out more carbon than humans. I saw that somewhere."

"That's not true, and also it's not what I'm arguing," Olivier said, aware that half the class had stopped pretending to take notes and was now just watching the way you watch two dogs figure out whether to fight. "I'm saying the planet needs the greenhouse effect. Without it we'd freeze. It's not evil. It's just gotten stronger than it should be."

"Then why do you even care," Trevor said, grinning like he'd found the crack. "If it's natural and good, what's the problem?"

This was the part Olivier had been dreading and also, he realized with a small jolt, the part where Trevor's whole argument quietly folded in on itself. Because Trevor was assuming that if a thing was natural, and had always existed, then more of it couldn't be a problem, that intensity didn't matter, only presence. Olivier turned that over for a second, the way you'd turn over a rock to see what's underneath.

"Without any of it," Olivier said slowly, working it out loud, feeling the shape of the sentence before he trusted it, "the average temperature on Earth would be about minus eighteen degrees. Right now it's around fifteen. That's the greenhouse effect, doing that, all sixty three degrees of difference. So no, it's not fake, and it's not evil either. You're half right, actually. It's not the existence of the thing that's the issue. It's that it's gotten stronger. Like turning up a blanket nobody asked to have turned up."

The room did that thing where it goes quiet not because everyone's impressed but because nobody knows if the argument's over. Mr. Aldrin, who had been leaning against the whiteboard eating what looked suspiciously like a granola bar disguised as chalk, straightened up.

"Interesting concession," he said to Trevor. "You said fake. Olivier's saying real, necessary, and currently too intense. Those aren't the same claim. Which one has evidence behind it?"

Trevor opened his mouth, closed it, and said, "I still think the volcano thing is substantive," which made absolutely no sense in context and made three people laugh, including Olivier, who hadn't meant to laugh at his own opponent mid debate but couldn't help it.

"It's not," Olivier said, still grinning, "but nice try." He didn't actually know, sitting there, whether he'd won on facts or just on the fact that Trevor had wandered off point about volcanic emissions, and he found himself wondering, half seriously, whether debate class ever really settled anything or just showed you which claims could survive being poked. The bell rang before anyone could answer that, and Trevor, gathering his notecards, muttered, "Fine, half right," in the tone of someone paying off a bet he still resented losing.

Nathaniel's laptop balanced on a stack of Marcus's textbooks, the screen glowing blue against the dim of the basement, where the air smelled like old carpet and the ranch popcorn Marcus's mom always left out in a chipped bowl.

"Okay, so a for loop just means it repeats," Marcus said, leaning back in his desk chair until it creaked dangerously. "You're telling the computer, do this thing, then do it again, then again, until I say stop."

"So it's like when your brother makes the same free throw ten times and thinks he's unstoppable," Nathaniel said, typing `for i in range(10):` and watching the cursor blink beneath it like it was waiting to be impressed.

"Kind of. Except code doesn't get cocky." Marcus grabbed a handful of popcorn. "Though mine sure does. Watch, I wrote a coin flip simulator last week for my stats project."

He pulled up his own file, ran it, and a column of H's and T's scrolled down the terminal. Somewhere in the middle sat five heads in a row, stacked like a tower nobody had bothered to knock down.

Nathaniel squinted at it. "Dude, doesn't that mean your code's broken? Five heads back to back seems like a lot."

"Nah, it's fair, I checked the function like four times."

"But five in a row." Nathaniel felt the pull of an idea he couldn't yet name, something about probability that his uncle liked to invoke every time he lost money at the casino, insisting the tables owed him a win because he'd been "due." His uncle would get despondent after every losing streak, sagging into his chair like the universe had implicated him personally, promised him something and then reneged.

"Let's just run it again," Marcus said, hitting the button. This time three heads, then a tail, then a jagged mess of both. He ran it once more, a hundred flips this time, and there, buried near flip sixty, sat six heads in a row.

"See," Nathaniel said slowly, feeling the shape of the thought sharpen, "either your code has some kind of bug that makes it clump heads together on purpose, or clumps like that just happen anyway, when you flip enough times."

"How would we even tell the difference?"

Nathaniel chewed his lip, staring at the screen the way he stared at word problems that seemed like tricks. "If the code were rigged, you'd think the coin would start acting different once it fell into heads, like it'd want to keep going. So what if we make it print out the actual chance calculated at flip fifty, right after a streak?"

They added a line, clumsy and inelegant, that printed the probability the function assigned to the next flip whenever the last five had matched. They ran it a dozen times. Every single time, after five heads, the printed number sat there stubborn and flat: 0.5. Never higher. Never lower. Not once did the streak seem to alter what came next.

"So it's not rigged," Marcus said, sounding almost disappointed, like he'd wanted to have written something clever by accident.

"It's not rigged," Nathaniel agreed. "The streak doesn't mean the coin owes you anything. It just means you flipped enough times that a streak was bound to show up somewhere." He thought of his uncle again, hunched over a roulette table insisting red was due after seven blacks, and wondered if anyone had ever shown him a hundred lines of scrolling H's and T's, and whether it would have mattered if they had.

Marcus swiveled his chair to face him, a grin spreading slow. "You're better at this than you think, you know that? You've been doing debugging for like twenty minutes and you're out here disproving your uncle's whole gambling philosophy."

"Somebody should tell him."

"Good luck. Print it out, mail it to Vegas."

They laughed, and Nathaniel typed a new line of code just to see it run, some strange rapport settling between the machine and his own stubborn curiosity, a friendship of sorts with the blinking cursor that asked nothing of him except that he keep asking questions.

Upstairs, Marcus's mom called down that dinner was ready, and neither of them moved right away, both still watching the heads and tails scroll past, waiting to see how long the next streak would be.

The computer lab smelled like burnt dust from the ancient projector, and Antoine had been staring at the same six lines of code for eleven minutes without blinking, which he was fairly sure was bad for his eyes.

```
def get_recommendation(video):
    if video.likes > 100:
        return True
    else:
        return False
```

"It's not running," he said to Priya, who sat beside him with her headphones around her neck like a horseshoe. "It just says syntax error and then it eviscerates my entire will to live."

"Dramatic," she said, not looking up from her own screen. "You're missing a colon somewhere. Or you indented wrong. Python's very particular about whitespace, it's basically a control freak."

Mr. Oyelaran, who taught the intro elective mostly by wandering the room and occasionally saying "hm" in a tone that could mean anything, had given them a simple assignment: build a toy program that decided whether a video should be "recommended" based on a made up engagement score. It was meant to be a gentle introduction to conditionals, nothing more, the kind of exercise that existed to make you comfortable typing `if` and `else` without setting anything on fire. But Antoine, who had spent the previous night falling down a two hour hole on his phone watching increasingly furious people argue about a celebrity breakup he did not care about, had gotten curious about something the assignment did not ask him to think about at all.

He added a second function, one that generated fake videos with fake stats, comments count, likes, average watch time, and a variable he decided to call `rage_bait`, set as a simple true or false flag he assigned at random. Then he told his program to sort the videos by predicted engagement and recommend whichever scored highest.

"Why does your rage bait thing keep winning," Priya asked, glancing over now, curious despite herself.

"I don't know. I didn't tell it to prefer them." He scrolled back through his own code, looking for the bug, assuming there was one, because there usually was. "I just made comments and watch time count more toward the score. I didn't touch the rage bait variable at all."

"So it's not actually about the rage bait," Priya said slowly. "It's that angry stuff probably gets more comments and watch time in your fake data. You set the numbers, not me."

He checked the little block where he'd generated the fake statistics, and she was right, embarrassingly right, the kind of right that made him feel both caught and oddly pleased. He had, without quite meaning to, made the angrier fake videos generate longer fake watch times and more fake comments, because that had simply felt realistic to him when he typed it, the way it feels realistic that a stove is hot. His program wasn't discovering some truth about human nature. It was returning exactly what he had built into it, a system faithfully reflecting its own assumptions back at him, true by the very shape of its definitions and therefore not proof of anything beyond itself.

"That's a little tautological, though, isn't it," he said, more to himself than to her, testing the word like a new shoe. "It only proves angry videos win because I decided angry videos get more engagement. I didn't prove the world works that way. I just assumed it and then acted surprised."

Priya shrugged, unbothered by the distinction in the way that people are unbothered by things they already half believed. "Sure, but think about your actual phone. Not the fake one. When's the last time your real feed got calmer the longer you scrolled?"

He thought about the celebrity breakup, the comments stacking into the thousands, the little thrill of outrage that had kept his thumb moving long after he stopped enjoying anything about it, and he had no good answer for her, which felt like its own kind of answer.

"I don't know if that's the same question," he said, choosing his words the way he'd choose a step on ice. "Whether the code proves something and whether the code matches something. Those aren't identical." He wasn't sure yet whether he was doing epistemology or just stalling on his homework, but the distinction between what a toy program demonstrates and what it merely assumes felt, suddenly, like the actual assignment, more than the colon he still hadn't fixed.

Mr. Oyelaran drifted past, glanced at Antoine's extra fifteen lines with mild interest, said "hm," and kept walking, offering no verdict either way. Antoine fixed the colon, watched the program run clean at last, and sat there a moment longer, not touching the keyboard, listening to the projector hum and thinking about how he was going to check, actually check, what his own phone did the next time he let it scroll for an hour uninterrupted.

The screen door slammed behind Elijah as he carried his grandfather's ancient laptop out to the porch, its fan wheezing like it had run a marathon just booting up.

"You sure this thing still works, Grandpa?" he asked, setting it on the wicker table between them.

His grandfather, retired after thirty years fixing mainframes nobody under fifty had heard of, snorted. "Works fine. You're the one who's never touched a line of code in his life."

"That's why I'm here." Elijah had signed up for an intro computer science class starting in the fall, and something in him, some mix of dread and hunger, wanted a head start before he showed up a total stranger to it all. He opened a text editor his grandfather had installed the night before and stared at the blinking cursor like it might blink back.

"Start simple," his grandfather said, leaning over with the particular satisfaction of a man about to be useful again. "Type print, parentheses, quotation marks, and something you want to say."

Elijah typed print("hello grandpa") and hit run, and the terminal spat back a syntax error in red, unforgiving text.

"You forgot the colon," his grandfather said, not unkindly, tapping the screen with a crooked finger. "Everything in here is picky. Computers don't do context clues. You say exactly what you mean or it throws the whole thing back at you."

Elijah fixed it, ran it again, and there it was: hello grandpa, printed clean and undeniable on the black screen. He laughed out loud, an actual bark of a laugh, and his grandfather grinned like Elijah had just landed a rocket on the moon instead of printed six characters of text.

"Feels kind of small," Elijah admitted, still smiling. "I thought coding was supposed to feel like magic."

"It is magic. You just did the equivalent of learning to say 'hello' in a language spoken by every machine on earth." His grandfather leaned back, chair creaking under him. "You know the first website ever put online was in 1991? Some physics lab in Switzerland. CERN."

Elijah looked up from the screen. "Wait, seriously? The whole internet started at a place that smashes atoms?"

"Not the internet. The web. Different thing, though nobody under thirty seems to know that." His grandfather scratched his chin. "And here's the part that ought to keep you up at night. The fella who invented it, Tim Berners-Lee, he could have locked the whole thing up. Patented it, licensed it, made every website ever built pay him a royalty. Instead he talked the lab into giving it away free in 1993. Royalty-free, forever."

Elijah sat with that for a second, fingers hovering over the keys. "So he just... gave up being a billionaire?"

"Something like that."

"That's either the most noble thing I've ever heard or the dumbest business decision in history," Elijah said, and he meant both halves of it. Some part of him, the part that had grown up watching startup founders get valorized on every screen he owned, wanted to call it a catastrophic financial blunder. Another part, quieter but stubborn, thought that if the web had come bundled with an invoice, maybe none of this, not this porch, not this laptop, not the two of them fumbling through a for-loop together, would exist in any recognizable form at all.

"Equivocal," his grandfather said suddenly, apropos of nothing, and Elijah blinked at him.

"What?"

"That's the word for how I feel about it, most days. Equivocal. Couldn't tell you whether it was a saintly move or a missed fortune, and I've had forty years to decide." He tapped the laptop. "Now debug your loop. It's stuck."

Elijah looked down and realized his for-loop had been running the whole time, silently, printing hello grandpa nine hundred times into a scroll of text that had swallowed the screen. He killed it, laughing, and his grandfather laughed too, wheezier than the fan but just as sincere.

"There's a real foreboding you get," Elijah said later, once the loop was fixed and capped at ten, "when the code just runs forever and you don't know why. Like it's going to keep going after I close the laptop. After I'm dead, even."

"Welcome to computer science," his grandfather said. "Every programmer who's ever lived has stared at a screen at two in the morning feeling exactly that."

Elijah typed one more line, ran it, and watched hello grandpa appear precisely ten times, no more, no less, obedient at last. He didn't know yet whether he'd major in this, whether the porch and the wheezing fan and the free, sprawling web that some Swiss lab let loose on the world would end up mattering to his life at all. But he saved the file anyway, named it something he'd remember, and left it open on the screen for morning.
